problem: Prior visual navigation methods fall short in different ways. Visual servoing is greedy, has a small convergence region and needs Image Jacobians. Visual MPC with sampling or gradient optimization (e.g., Finn & Levine) is too slow for real-time use. Learned visual path-following methods (Zero-shot Visual Imitation, Visual Memory for Path Following, imitation learning) do not explicitly penalize untraversable areas, so they collide with obstacles that were not on the recorded route.
motivation: RGB cameras are cheap and robust compared with lidar or depth sensors. Following a route given as a list of images, without a map or localization, is natural and lets routes be recorded in simulation and executed in the real world. The key observation is that MPC over a learned image predictor can balance trajectory following against collision avoidance, but solving it online is non-convex and too slow; the optimization can instead be amortized into a feed-forward policy trained by backpropagating the MPC cost through differentiable, frozen models.
key_idea: PoliNet, a small CNN, maps the current 360° image and the next subgoal image to N=8 future velocity commands. It is trained to minimize a visual-MPC cost (image loss + traversability loss + reference loss) by backpropagating through a frozen 360° view-synthesis model (VUNet-360) and a frozen traversability estimator (GONet), so no prediction or optimization is needed at test time.
insight: The MPC optimization can be amortized into a network that is both cheap and competitive in cost. In Table I, PoliNet reaches J=0.277 (sim) / 0.214 (real), comparable to 20-iteration backprop MPC (0.270 / 0.236), while running at 72.25 Hz with 325 MB versus 0.14 Hz with 1752 MB. Online optimizers restricted to the 3 Hz real-time budget (backprop nit=2, CEM M=10) get 0.000 success in navigation (Table II). The traversability weight is critical and must be balanced (Table V): with weight 0 success falls to about 0.78–0.81 and J_trav rises to 0.161; with weight 1.0 the policy becomes over-conservative, avoids narrow passages and gets ~0 success; 0.5 gives 0.997/0.850. Predicting all 8 future 360° frames in parallel from the raw image, blending front and back fisheye views, beats both serial prediction and the original VUNet (Table VII: L1 0.088 vs 0.113–0.132, SSIM 0.676 vs 0.543–0.581) and runs faster (19.28 Hz vs 5.03 Hz).
method: Task setup: the route is a sequence of K subgoal 360° images, each stored as a front/back pair of 180° fisheye images at 128×128. The robot switches to the next subgoal when the absolute pixel difference falls below d_th = k_th·(initial difference), with k_th = 0.7. No map, localization or planner is used.

Visual MPC cost: J = J_img + κ1·J_trav + κ2·J_ref, with κ1 = 0.5 and κ2 = 0.1. J_img is the weighted mean L1 difference between the subgoal and the N predicted images (w_i = 1, w_N = 5, which allows detours but enforces final convergence). J_trav is the mean of (1 − clip(κ_trav·p_trav))², with κ_trav = 1.1, using GONet traversability on the predicted front images. J_ref is the squared difference to the teleoperator velocities and serves as a smoothness regularizer.

VUNet-360 predictive model: an encoder-decoder (8 conv + 8 deconv layers) takes the front image and the flipped back image, concatenates N=8 virtual (v, ω) pairs into the latent vector, and outputs flows and visibility masks for all N steps in parallel. A blending module bilinearly samples both the front and back input images and fuses them with softmax masks to predict each future front/back image. It is trained with multi-step L1 loss on teleoperation data.

PoliNet policy: an 8-layer CNN with batch norm and leaky ReLU takes the concatenated current and subgoal front/back images. It outputs 2×N values passed through tanh and scaled to ±v_max = 0.5 m/s and ±ω_max = 1.0 rad/s. The horizon is N = 8 at 3 Hz, i.e., 2.667 s.

Training PoliNet as a learned MPC: VUNet-360 and GONet are frozen, and the cost J is backpropagated to PoliNet only. The subgoal is a random future frame t+k with k ≤ N_r = 12 from the teleoperation data. Training uses Adam (lr 1e-4) with sim and real data balanced equally. At test time only PoliNet runs, at 72.25 Hz.

setting.backbone: PoliNet (8-layer CNN, trained from scratch) optimized through frozen VUNet-360 (view synthesis, trained on own data) and GONet (traversability estimator from prior work)
setting.training_data: Own teleoperation data. Real: 10.30 h of 360° RGB and velocity commands from 12 Stanford buildings (8 train / 2 val / 2 test). Sim: 3.59 h in 36 GibsonEnv buildings (Stanford 2D-3D-S + Matterport3D), split into 2.79 h train from 26 buildings, 0.32 h val from 5, 0.48 h test from 5. Sim and real data are balanced equally during training.
setting.observation: 360° RGB (Ricoh THETA S, two 180° fisheye images resized to 128×128), plus the visual trajectory of subgoal 360° images
setting.action_space: continuous linear/angular velocity; 8-step velocity sequence predicted at 3 Hz (|v| ≤ 0.5 m/s, |ω| ≤ 1.0 rad/s)
setting.simulator: GibsonEnv (Stanford 2D-3D-S and Matterport3D models) + real world
setting.privileged: none. Subgoal image poses are used only for evaluation; the visual trajectory is recorded beforehand (by teleoperation or a virtual camera) and is the task input.

results: In GibsonEnv (Cases A–C, 100 noisy trials each), PoliNet reaches SR/coverage/SPL of 0.997/0.999/0.996 without obstacles and 0.850/0.916/0.850 with unseen obstacles. The strongest baseline, Visual Memory for Path Following (0.858/0.740 SR/SPL, 0.800/0.688 with obstacles), was run without collision detection. ZVI gets 0.433/0.307 SR and IL (N=1) 0.320/0.297. Over 10 environments PoliNet averages 0.979 / 0.865 SR versus ZVI 0.574 / 0.463 and IL (N=8) 0.276 / 0.313. On the real robot it reaches 1.00 SR without obstacles and 0.80 with obstacles on 24.1 m and 16.1 m routes (IL N=8: 0.10–0.90), and 0.80–0.90 SR for sim-to-real trajectories. Online MPC optimizers that fit the 3 Hz budget score 0 SR.
limitations: Traversability is only a soft cost and the horizon is short (2.667 s), so the robot cannot plan long detours and occasionally fails around large obstacles; large obstacles filling the subgoal view also hurt convergence.
The route must be pre-recorded as a dense image trajectory and subgoal switching relies on a hand-tuned pixel-difference threshold. This is a path-following setting, not goal search or exploration.
The evaluation uses a small number of custom scenes (3–10 sim cases, 2 real routes, 3 sim-to-real routes) with no standard benchmark, and one baseline was evaluated without collision detection.
